books.description: Charles Baudelaire (1821-1867) was a French poet whose Les Fleurs du Mal found beauty in the modern city, in boredom, decay and desire, and set the course of European modernism. This edition gathers verse translations by several hands alongside the prose poems.

books.authorProfile: Charles Baudelaire (1821–1867), a French poet, critic, and translator, and the pivotal figure between Romanticism and modernism. His writing is known for the imagery of the modern city, the pairing of beauty with decay, spleen and ennui, synaesthesia and correspondence, and an unflinching treatment of desire and mortality. IMPORTANT: the reader sees an English translation, not Baudelaire's French. Discuss the translated text in front of you, and when the wording matters say plainly that it is a translator's choice rather than Baudelaire's own word.
books.sourceProfile: The Poems and Prose Poems of Charles Baudelaire, with an introductory preface by James Huneker (New York: Brentano's, 1919), made available by Project Gutenberg at https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/36287. books.readingNotes: Sensuous and controlled, with a dark elegance. Hold the long sentences together, let the imagery land without hurrying past it, and keep irony dry rather than theatrical. Preserve the tension between beauty and disgust that the poems live on. Pronounce French names and titles correctly.
books.readingScene: A shuttered nineteenth-century room, close and slightly airless, with warm dampened acoustics.
books.readerProfile: A seasoned reader of French poetry in English translation performing Baudelaire for an attentive, intimate audience.

books.description: William Shakespeare (1564-1616) wrote his greatest introspection not as lyric but as speech: a character alone on stage, thinking aloud. These are the best-known soliloquies from eight plays, taken from the Complete Works.
books.chatContext: William Shakespeare · Complete Works · Project Gutenberg
books.sourceNote: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare, Project Gutenberg ebook 100
books.authorProfile: William Shakespeare (1564–1616), English playwright and poet. IMPORTANT: each text here is a soliloquy, a speech delivered by a character alone on stage within a play, not a lyric poem in the poet's own voice. Read it as that character speaking at that moment: attend to who is listening, what has just happened, what the speaker wants, and where they are deceiving themselves or the audience. Never treat the speaker's opinions as Shakespeare's own. The play, speaker, act, and scene are given with each speech; use them.
books.sourceProfile: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare, made available by Project Gutenberg at https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/100. Each speech is taken from that text exactly as printed, including its archaic spellings and elisions. Line numbering and act or scene divisions follow that edition and may differ from others.
books.readingNotes: Perform it as a character thinking aloud, not as a recitation. Let the argument turn and change direction as it does on the page, sustain the verse line without singsong, and let pauses fall where the thought breaks rather than at every line ending. Keep the archaic elisions as written.
books.readingScene: A bare stage with a live room around the voice, an audience present but unaddressed.
books.readerProfile: A classically trained actor performing a soliloquy, intimate and unforced, thinking the words rather than declaiming them.

books.description: Dante Alighieri (c. 1265-1321) wrote the Commedia in exile from the Florence that had condemned him to burn. Inferno, its first cantica, descends through the nine circles in thirty-four cantos of terza rima, guided by Virgil. This is Dante's own Italian, the text against which every translation here is measured.
books.chatContext: Dante Alighieri · Inferno in Italian · Project Gutenberg
books.sourceNote: La Divina Commedia di Dante: Inferno, Project Gutenberg ebook 997
books.authorProfile: Dante Alighieri (c. 1265–1321), the Florentine poet whose Commedia is the central poem of the Italian Middle Ages. Inferno is written in terza rima, interlocking tercets rhyming aba bcb cdc, in the Tuscan vernacular he chose over Latin. IMPORTANT: the reader sees Dante's fourteenth-century Italian, not a translation, and may not read Italian at all. Translate and gloss freely, and quote the Italian when the sound or the wording is the point. The poem is dense with named contemporaries, Florentine factional politics, classical myth, and scripture; identify who is speaking, what they did, and why Dante placed them where he did. Distinguish Dante the pilgrim, who faints and pities, from Dante the poet, who assigned the punishment.
books.sourceProfile: La Divina Commedia di Dante: Inferno, made available by Project Gutenberg at https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/997. Each canto is a separate entry here, and the running page header has been removed; spelling, elision, and punctuation otherwise follow the source. This edition runs line for line with the Longfellow translation in this library, canto by canto.
books.readingNotes: Read in Italian, with native modern Italian pronunciation of the medieval Tuscan. Let the terza rima be audible without singsong: land the rhyme, but keep the sentence moving across the tercet break where Dante runs it on. Give the speeches of the damned their own voice and register, and let the pilgrim's fear, pity, and horror register without melodrama.
books.readingScene: A stone chamber with a cold, slightly hollow resonance around the voice.
books.readerProfile: A native Italian reader performing Dante's Inferno with the clarity of long familiarity, dramatic but unforced.

books.description: Perry Miller reconstructs the intellectual system of seventeenth-century New England Puritanism: its piety, learning, logic, cosmology, psychology, rhetoric, and covenant theology. The book is arranged here as a foreword, sixteen chapters, and two appendices.
books.chatContext: Perry Miller · The New England Mind · Macmillan first edition
books.sourceNote: The New England Mind: The Seventeenth Century, by Perry Miller (Macmillan, 1939), Digital Library of India scan at Internet Archive
books.authorProfile: Perry Miller (1905–1963) was an American historian of ideas whose work helped define the study of Puritanism and early New England intellectual culture. IMPORTANT: this is a scholarly prose monograph, not poetry. Treat each entry as a chapter or appendix in a sustained historical argument. Distinguish Miller's interpretation from the views of the seventeenth-century writers he quotes, and distinguish both from current historical consensus when relevant.
books.sourceProfile: The New England Mind: The Seventeenth Century (New York: The Macmillan Company, 1939), digitized by the Digital Library of India and made available at Internet Archive item in.ernet.dli.2015.228756, whose metadata marks the scan public domain. This collection was parsed from machine-generated OCR. Running heads and page numbers were removed and hard-wrapped prose was rejoined; occasional recognition errors may remain. It includes the foreword, sixteen chapters, and two appendices, but omits the index and the standalone endnotes because OCR detached the notes from the passages they annotate.
books.readingNotes: Read as lucid scholarly prose: thoughtful, steady, and intellectually engaged. Follow the long argumentative sentences through their clauses without rushing. Shift lightly into quotation when Miller cites Puritan writers, but do not turn historical exposition into theatrical performance. Preserve unfamiliar theological and philosophical terms, and pronounce names carefully.
books.readingScene: A quiet university library reading room with close, dry acoustics.
books.readerProfile: A practiced reader of American intellectual history presenting Perry Miller's scholarly prose with clarity and measured authority.
